summary.text: Sharks are cartilaginous fish with a ribless skeleton, five to seven gill slits on each side, and skin covered in protective scales called denticles.
They range from the 17-centimetre dwarf lanternshark to the whale shark, the largest fish in the world, and are common down to 2,000 metres.
Several species, such as the great white and tiger shark, are apex predators, while the whale shark and basking shark are filter-feeders that eat plankton.

facts.label: Where found
facts.value: All seas, commonly down to 2,000 metres

facts.label: Old name
facts.value: Mariners called sharks "sea dogs" until the 16th century

items.prompt: Tiny placoid scales cover a shark's skin. What do they do for the shark?

options.label: They store fat that lets the shark float at one depth
They shield the skin from damage and parasites and help water flow past
They let the shark take in oxygen through its skin
They anchor the shark's replaceable teeth in place

items.explain: The denticles protect the skin from damage and parasites and improve the shark's fluid dynamics.

items.prompt: A boat crew sees a huge shark gliding slowly through a cloud of tiny drifting animals with its mouth open. Which is it most likely?

options.label: A great white shark hunting seals
A hammerhead shark scanning the sea floor
A mako shark chasing fast fish
A whale shark or basking shark

items.explain: The whale shark and basking shark are filter-feeding planktivores, while the great white, hammerhead and mako are listed among the apex predators.

items.prompt: A shark turns up far up a river, in water with no salt. Sharks generally stay in the sea, so what could explain this?

options.label: A few species, such as the bull shark, live in both seawater and fresh water
Every shark species spends part of its life in rivers
It followed prey upstream, since sharks cannot sense salt
It is a juvenile of a deep sea species that drifted in

items.explain: Sharks generally do not live in freshwater, but exceptions include the bull shark and river sharks, which can live in either, and the Ganges shark, which lives only in freshwater.

items.prompt: Shark numbers have fallen sharply in recent decades. What is the main cause?

options.label: Warming seas that wiped out their prey
Loss of the plankton the whale shark eats
Overfishing, including the practice of finning
Competition with bony fish for food

items.explain: Since 1970 shark populations have dropped by 71%, mostly from overfishing and practices such as shark finning.

items.prompt: Why might some small sharks be called "dogfish"?

options.label: They make a barking sound underwater to find one another
Sailors called sharks "sea dogs", and the name stuck to some species
They hunt in coordinated packs much as wolves do
They were first kept as pets in harbour towns

items.explain: Until the 16th century sharks were known to mariners as sea dogs, and that is still evident in several species termed dogfish.

items.prompt: Sharks largely took over from another shark-like group that had dominated the Triassic and Early Jurassic. Which group was it?

options.label: Hybodonts
Rays and skates
Chimaeras
Acanthodians

items.explain: During the Jurassic true sharks diversified and largely replaced the hybodonts.

paragraphs.heading: What makes a shark
paragraphs.text: Sharks are cartilaginous fish with a skeleton that has no ribs, five to seven gill slits per side, and pectoral fins that are not joined to the head. Their skin is covered in placoid scales, or denticles, which guard against damage and parasites and improve how they move through water. They also carry many sets of teeth that can be replaced. Modern sharks form a group called Selachii, whose closest relatives are the rays and skates.

paragraphs.heading: Where sharks live
paragraphs.text: Sharks live in every sea and are common down to 2,000 metres. They range from the dwarf lanternshark, a deep-sea fish just 17 centimetres long, to the whale shark, the biggest fish in the world at roughly 12 to 18.8 metres. Most avoid fresh water, but there are exceptions. The bull shark and the river sharks move between salt and fresh water, and the Ganges shark lives in fresh water alone.

paragraphs.heading: Hunters and grazers
paragraphs.text: Several sharks are apex predators, animals at the very top of their food chain. Examples include the great white, tiger, bull, mako, thresher, Greenland and hammerhead sharks. Others feed by straining plankton from the water. The whale shark and basking shark eat this way, and they rank among the largest fish that have ever lived.

paragraphs.heading: A long history
paragraphs.text: Shark-like fish such as Cladoselache appeared in the Devonian, 419 to 359 million years ago, and some fossil scales resembling those of cartilaginous fish are older still. The earliest confirmed modern sharks date from the Early Jurassic, around 200 million years ago, though true sharks may reach back to the Permian. During the Jurassic they branched out into many forms. They largely took the place of the hybodonts, shark-like fish that had dominated before them.

paragraphs.heading: The shark family tree
paragraphs.text: Sharks sit within a larger group that also holds the rays and skates, and that group sits within the cartilaginous fish, alongside the chimaeras. Scientists once thought some sharks were closer to rays than to other sharks, which would mean sharks were not one natural group. Current molecular studies instead back sharks and the rays and skates as separate single groups. Modern sharks divide into two superorders, Galeomorphi and Squalomorphi.

paragraphs.heading: A few shark orders
paragraphs.text: Ground sharks include the blue, tiger, bull and oceanic whitetip sharks, along with catsharks and hammerheads. They have a long snout and a nictitating membrane that shields the eyes during an attack. Mackerel sharks include the great white, the makos, the threshers and the goblin and megamouth sharks. The frilled shark, from yet another order, looks a little like a sea snake.

paragraphs.heading: Sea dogs in trouble
paragraphs.text: Until the 16th century, sailors called sharks sea dogs, a name that lives on in fish called dogfish. Where the word shark comes from is unclear; it may come from a Dutch word for a villain. People catch sharks for their meat and fins. Since 1970 shark numbers have fallen by 71%, mostly through overfishing and the cutting off of fins.
